title: Fact Both Ways
context: Grade 4, and this is the topic where the chapter stops adding methods and says what its two words actually mean. An adult sees the same division written twice. What is being fixed is a word with nothing attached to it: a child who says six is a factor, full stop, has said nothing, because six is a factor of thirty and is not a factor of twenty. The printed page is loose here in exactly that way, calling a multiple the product of two or more factors without ever saying of what, so the gate is doing the work the wording does not.

writeup.why: Read one exact division from both ends at once, and learn to say what each number is a factor of, or a multiple of.
writeup.look: A turning card in the middle with both of its readings held side by side, a size rail under it and a word pad at the edge.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Fact Both Ways' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the readings written against the readings this phase has to write, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each sentence is completed with its number named and the second fixed at what the phase asks for. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The card stands in the middle of the top of the working area, 424 by 216 at 395,202, carrying one exact division written out in full. A tap turns it about its upright, one face stating the fact about factors and the other the fact about multiples, and once it has been turned both faces are lifted out and held side by side inside a single drawn frame, 880 by 216 at 167,202, with a hairline between them rather than a wall: they are one fact and the frame says so. The name it gate guards the writing bay below, 520 by 164 at 64,442: a sentence is laid out as tiles with an empty slot in it, and the word tiles reading factor and multiple will not drop until a number tile naming what they belong to has been placed. A sentence left with its slot open springs back with the slot lit and nothing marked. The size rail runs under the card, 880 by 92 at 167,442, drawn strictly to scale from nothing at its left to the greater of the two numbers at its right, with each number standing at its own distance along it and the factor slot drawn at the smaller end; a bigger number dragged into that slot is refused and the rail is redrawn at scale so that the two lengths are the whole of the explanation. The pair bay sits at the left of the lower half, 520 by 164 at 64,606, laying two numbers out as equal rows on a ruled board and returning the number they build on a card labelled as the multiple of both. The own list bay takes the right of the lower half, 500 by 164 at 616,606: one penned factor list with a wall past its last card, and beside it a track of multiples leaving the frame at the right hand edge with no end mark and no last step drawn, and one number lighting in both of them at once. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a quotient or a built number is asked for, and beside them a word pad carrying the chapter's four words, factor, multiple, finite and infinite, turned towards a partner for the flashcard quiz and answered by press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number built by multiplying is green, anything standing in both lists at once is rose, whatever is left over and any trial that fails is vermilion, the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber, and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a leftover is told by standing outside the rows before it is told by a band, and a list that stops is told by the wall at each end of it and a list that does not by the open edge of the frame. Turning the card never replaces one reading with the other. The first face stays up and the second joins it, because the moment one of the two is taken down the child is back to holding two separate things to remember instead of one fact read from either end.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last division the child turned, both of its readings still up, with the size rail drawn underneath.

phases.win: both readings stand in one frame and each names the number it belongs to
phases.does: turns the card, reads each face, and holds the two up together
phases.goal: one exact division makes a factor fact and a multiple fact at once
phases.says: Which one is the factor and which is the multiple? One division tells you both.
phases.check: 13 divides 52 exactly. Say that as a fact about factors and then as a fact about multiples, naming both numbers each time.
phases.feels: one division, and both sentences were true before either of them was written
phases.hands: Write one exact division on the board, seventy-eight divided by six is thirteen, and under it rule two lines. Have the class fill the first line with a sentence using the word factor and the second with a sentence using the word multiple, and insist that each sentence names both numbers. Then rub out the two numbers in one sentence and ask whether it still says anything at all.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers is doing the dividing? Second rung, the phase's: which number is being divided, and what is it to the other one? Third rung: the card is cut to a small division and the child turns it and reads both faces aloud. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the page's own wording calls a multiple the product of two or more factors and never says of what, so the word is met with nothing attached to it and is repeated back the same way.
wrong.move: says that six is a factor and stops there, without ever naming what it is a factor of.
wrong.screen: the gate holds the sentence open with its empty slot lit and nothing marked. Two further cards are laid beside it, one where six divides thirty with nothing left over and one where six is tried on twenty and two are set outside the rows, and both are read out as sentences with their numbers in. The child's half sentence stays exactly where it was built.

wrong.why: the bigger number is the one the question started from and the two words were met on the same day, so which of them attaches to which number is a coin toss.
wrong.move: writes it the other way round, calling seventy-eight a factor of six.
wrong.screen: the size rail is drawn to scale with six standing near its left hand end and seventy-eight at its right, and the factor slot at the smaller end turns the bigger number back with the two lengths left drawn. Both faces of the card are then held up in the frame together, each naming its own number, and the child's sentence stays in the writing bay beside them.

phases.screen: a card showing one exact division with both faces still blank
phases.soWhat: If one number divides another exactly, the first is a factor of the second and the second is a multiple of the first.
phases.concept: Two words for the two ends of one division

phases.win: the built number appears labelled as the multiple of both numbers in the pair
phases.does: lays the pair out as rows and reads off the number they come to
phases.goal: the product of a factor pair is the multiple those factors belong to
phases.says: These two are a pair. What is the number they build to them?
phases.check: 4 and 6 are a factor pair of 24. Write what 24 is to 4, and what it is to 6.
phases.feels: the number a pair builds belongs to both of them at once
phases.hands: Give each pair of children two number cards that multiply to something under a hundred, three and nineteen for instance, and a pile of counters. Build the rows, count the total, and write the number they built on a third card. Then ask each pair for two true sentences about their third card, one for each of the two numbers that built it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what do those two numbers build? Second rung, the phase's: does each of them divide what they built? Third rung: the pair bay is cut to a small pair, the child lays it out and reads the total. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: fifty-seven is the number that was made, and the thing that was made is easy to hear as the thing that belongs to the two numbers that made it.
wrong.move: calls fifty-seven a factor of three and of nineteen, turning the relation the wrong way round.
wrong.screen: the pair bay lays three rows of nineteen out on the ruled board and the built card is read out as what those rows come to. The size rail is drawn under it to scale with all three numbers standing along it, and the factor slot at the smaller end takes each of the two small numbers in turn and turns the built number back. Nothing the child wrote is cleared.

wrong.why: the bigger number looks as though it did most of the work, and the smaller one reads as a multiplier rather than as a factor in its own right.
wrong.move: says the number belongs only to the bigger of the two that built it, because nineteen is nearer to fifty-seven.
wrong.screen: both divisions are run on the ruled board one under the other, fifty-seven into three rows and fifty-seven into nineteen rows, each drawn genuinely equal with the leftover shelf beside it staying empty. The two sentences are then written under their own boards, and the child's single sentence stays where it was put with its slot for the second number lit.

phases.screen: the pair bay holding two numbers with the built number still empty
phases.soWhat: The product of a factor pair is the multiple of both numbers in the pair.
phases.concept: A factor pair and the number it builds

phases.win: the bigger number is turned back on the rail and the smaller one settles in the slot
phases.does: tries the bigger number in the factor slot, then puts the smaller one in
phases.goal: a bigger number cannot be a factor of a smaller one
phases.says: Try the bigger one as the factor. Look at the rail and say what goes wrong.
phases.check: Can 96 be a factor of 12? Can 12 be a factor of 12? Say why for each.
phases.feels: the rail says it before any dividing does
phases.hands: Put thirty-five counters in one heap and twenty-one in another. Ask whether thirty-five could be a factor of twenty-one, and let somebody try to make even one row of thirty-five out of the smaller heap. Then ask whether seven is a factor of both, and build those rows too. Finish by asking whether twenty-one is a factor of twenty-one, and build that one as well.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the two numbers is the bigger? Second rung, the phase's: can a bigger number go into a smaller one even once? Third rung: the rail is cut to two small numbers and the child puts each of them into the factor slot in turn. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the two numbers really are connected, seven really does divide both, and a relation that exists gets attached to whichever question was asked.
wrong.move: answers yes because seven divides both of them, so the two numbers look related enough for either word.
wrong.screen: the rail is drawn to scale with seven near the left hand end and both of the others further along. Seven is dropped into the factor slot against thirty-five and settles, then against twenty-one and settles again, and the true sentence is written out for each. Thirty-five is then dropped into the factor slot against twenty-one and is turned back, with its length on the rail left drawn past the other number.

wrong.why: the half of the rule that is remembered is the half that was surprising, and less than or EQUAL TO loses its second half within a day of being read.
wrong.move: refuses to let twenty-one be a factor of twenty-one, because a factor was said to be smaller.
wrong.screen: the rail is drawn with both markers landing on exactly the same point along it, and the division runs on the board as one row holding all twenty-one with the leftover shelf beside it drawn empty and read out as empty. The rule on the word pad opens with the equal half lit, and the child's refusal stays in the answer slot beside it.

phases.screen: the size rail with two numbers on it and the factor slot waiting
phases.soWhat: A factor is never greater than the number it belongs to, though it may be equal to it.
phases.concept: A factor is never the bigger one

phases.win: the same number lights at the closed end of the pen and at the start of the track
phases.does: drops one number into both lists and reads where it lands in each
phases.goal: a number is its own greatest factor and its own smallest multiple
phases.says: Put it in both lists. Where does it sit in one, and where in the other?
phases.check: Where does 44 stand in its own list of factors, and where in its own list of multiples?
phases.feels: the same number shuts one list and opens the other
phases.hands: Take seventeen and write its factors on one side of the board and the first few of its multiples on the other, leaving the multiple list open with nothing after the last one. Ask a child to ring the same number in both lists. Then do it again with forty-four, which has six factors rather than two, and ask whether the ringed number moved.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is standing at the shut end of the pen? Second rung, the phase's: which number is the first step of the track? Third rung: the bay is cut to a small number, the child fills both lists and rings what stands in each. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: a list of a number's factors is heard as a list of the numbers that go into it, and a thing is not usually counted among the things that make it up.
wrong.move: leaves the number out of both of its own lists, because its own lists sound like lists of other numbers.
wrong.screen: the own list bay lights the shut end of the pen and the first step of the track at the same instant, with the same number card standing in each. The two claims are then run in front of the child: the number divided by itself, drawn as one row with nothing outside it, and one step of the number, drawn landing on it. The child's two lists stay exactly as they were written.

wrong.why: the whole chapter has been setting the two words against each other, one list closing in and the other running out, so a number standing in both reads as a contradiction rather than as the place where they meet.
wrong.move: says a number cannot be in both lists at once, because factor and multiple sound like opposites, and drops it from whichever was written second.
wrong.screen: the pen and the track are drawn side by side with the number lit in both and a hairline joining the two marks. The pen is read from its left post to its wall, ending on the number, and the track is read from its first step outward, starting on the number and leaving the frame. Nothing is removed from either list.

phases.screen: the own list bay with a penned factor list and a running track side by side
phases.soWhat: A number is its own greatest factor and its own smallest multiple.
phases.concept: A number stands at both ends of its own list

writeup.delight: The first phase, at the turn. The card goes over once and the two faces do not take turns: the first one lifts clear and slides to the left of the frame while the second rises into the right of it, and for the length of that movement the division itself is drawn joining them, the same numbers running through both sentences. Drag either reading and the other comes with it, hinged, because neither was found without the other. Try to lift one out of the frame on its own and it will not come, and the hairline between the two lights instead of any warning being spoken.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase one exact division stands on the card in the middle of the stage with both of its written faces still blank and the frame beside it empty and ruled for two. On the second the pair bay holds two numbers with the ruled board between them bare and the built number still an empty card. On the third the size rail is drawn to scale with two numbers standing along it and the factor slot at its smaller end waiting. On the fourth the own list bay is open with a penned factor list on the left, both of its walls up, and a track of multiples on the right leaving the frame with no end mark, and one number card lying between them. The running count at the top left holds the readings written against the readings this phase has to write, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the card, or the empty built number, or the factor slot, or the number card lying between the two lists, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which of the two numbers is the one doing the dividing. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any exact division on the card, with the size rail live, the pair bay open and the word pad turned towards a partner. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming which number is the factor and which the multiple, building a number from a pair, refusing a factor bigger than its number, and finding the number that closes one list and opens the other.
voiceLines: One division on a card. It has another face, and both of them are true.
Which one is the factor and which is the multiple? One division tells you both.
These two are a pair. What is the number they build to them?
Try the bigger one as the factor. Look at the rail and say what goes wrong.
Put it in both lists. Where does it sit in one, and where in the other?
A new division on the card. Read it from one end, then from the other.
Free play. Any exact division on the card, the rail live, the word pad turned over.
Say it again, and this time say which number it belongs to.
Every card turned, and never once a word left hanging with no number on it.

observations.why: Dividing exactly is one relation between two numbers, and the two words simply name its two ends.
observations.soWhat: Knowing that one number divides another is already knowing both facts.
observations.observe: One division produced two sentences and no second piece of work was done for the second one.

observations.why: A number is a factor of something and a multiple of something, so the word on its own says nothing at all.
observations.soWhat: Always say what a number is a factor of, or a multiple of.
observations.observe: Neither word would go into a sentence until a number had been named for it.

observations.why: A factor has to go into the number, and a number bigger than it cannot go in even once.
observations.soWhat: A factor is never greater than the number it belongs to, though it may be equal to it.
observations.observe: The rail turned the bigger number back every time it was offered as the factor.

observations.why: A number divides itself exactly, and one step of it lands on itself.
observations.soWhat: A number is its own greatest factor and its own smallest multiple.
observations.observe: The same number lit at the shut end of one list and at the first step of the other.

description: Turn one exact division over and read it from both ends, and never say either word without naming the number it belongs to.

source_tool.description: One exact division sits in the middle of the stage on a card that turns over. One face reads it as a fact about factors and the other as a fact about multiples, and once it has been turned both faces stay up together in a frame, because the point is that they are one fact and not two. A name it gate sits in front of the writing bay: the words factor and multiple cannot be dropped into a sentence until the number they belong to has been named, and a sentence left hanging is handed back with the missing number lit. A size rail runs under the card with the smaller number at one end and the bigger at the other, and the factor slot will only accept the smaller one; a bigger number dragged into it is turned back with the rail drawn to scale so that the reason is visible rather than stated. A pair bay takes two numbers, multiplies them out as rows and hands back the number they build, labelled as the multiple of that pair. An own list bay puts one number at the top of its own penned factor list and at the foot of its own running track at the same time, which is the one place where the two lists touch. A word pad holds the chapter's four words for a partner to be quizzed on.
source_tool.art_direction: A turning card above a size rail / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: trays of countable things, ruled rows on a board, a ladder of rungs with one trial to a rung, a pen with a wall at each end, a track of equal steps, cards that turn over, and two rings of cord that overlap.

Equal groups are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a row is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are in it, and the rows are kept apart by a drawn wall or a plain gap and never by colour alone.

Whatever is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the rows, on the same surface, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never crossed out, never tucked under a row and never left to be guessed from a gap. The leftover is the reason a trial failed, so it is the last thing any stage may hide.

A list of factors is drawn penned in between one and the number itself, with both ends of the run plainly stopped by a wall or a final post, so the list can be seen to end. A list of multiples is drawn running from the number away to the right, and the track carrying it leaves the frame with no end mark and no last step drawn, so the list can be seen not to end. The two never run the same way on one stage.

A run of trials is drawn unbroken. Every whole number from one up to the last one tried keeps its own rung or row, in order, with none left out, and a trial that fails is drawn and marked as a failure rather than dropped.
Where the digits of a number are added, every digit sits in its own cell, zeros included, and a cell holding a zero is drawn and counted in rather than left out of the line.
Nothing the child is asked to count one at a time comes to more than twenty things in one group. A larger quantity is a ruled array of identical tiles or a written numeral, never a loose heap.
A list is told apart by the wall or the open edge at its end first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a counter or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number that is built by multiplying is green, and anything standing in both lists at once is rose, and those three hold in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Whatever is left over, and any trial that fails, is vermilion; the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber; and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. All of that holds in greyscale, because a failed trial is told apart by the leftover drawn outside its row before it is told apart by colour, and a factor list is told apart from a list of multiples by the wall at each end of it before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.

voice.onNext: A new division on the card. Read it from one end, then from the other.
voice.opening: One division on a card. It has another face, and both of them are true.
voice.onFinish: Every card turned, and never once a word left hanging with no number on it.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any exact division on the card, the rail live, the word pad turned over.

phase_map.concept: Two words for the two ends of one division
A factor pair and the number it builds
A factor is never the bigger one
A number stands at both ends of its own list

placement.where: After both lists have been built by hand for one number, so there is something for the two words to be about. The tool is what holds both readings of one division up at the same moment, which writing can only do by putting them on two lines and hoping they are read together.

answer_key.rule: If one number divides another exactly, the first is a factor of the second and the second is a multiple of the first. That is one fact read from two ends, and no second piece of work is needed to get the other half. The product of a factor pair is the multiple those two factors belong to. A factor is always less than or equal to the number it divides, so a bigger number can never be a factor of a smaller one. A number is the greatest factor of itself and the smallest multiple of itself. Always say what a number is a factor of, or a multiple of, because neither word means anything on its own.
answer_key.wrong: The card turns back over slowly with the division drawn as rows underneath, the size rail is redrawn to scale, and the hanging sentence is shown with the missing number lit. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 78 divided by 6 is 13 with nothing over, so the division is exact.
The number that does the dividing is the factor, so 6 is a factor of 78.
The number being divided is the multiple, so 78 is a multiple of 6, and one division said both.
items.answer: 6 is a factor of 78, and 78 is a multiple of 6
items.question: 6 divides 78 exactly. Which of the two is the factor and which is the multiple?
items.checkpoint: One exact division makes a factor fact and a multiple fact at the same time.
items.misconception: Saying that 6 is a factor and stopping there, without naming what it is a factor of.

steps: 3 times 19 is 57, so the two numbers multiply to give 57.
Both of them divide 57 exactly, so both are factors of it.
The number a factor pair builds is the multiple those two factors belong to.
items.answer: Their multiple: 57 is a multiple of 3 and a multiple of 19
items.question: 3 and 19 are a factor pair of 57. What is 57 to them?
items.checkpoint: The product of a factor pair is the multiple of both numbers in the pair.
items.misconception: Calling 57 a factor of 3 and 19, which turns the relation the wrong way round.

steps: A factor has to divide the number exactly and leave nothing over.
35 is bigger than 21, so it cannot go into 21 even once.
A factor is always less than or equal to the number it divides, and 21 is not a multiple of 35 either.
items.question: Could 35 be a factor of 21?
items.checkpoint: A factor is never greater than the number it belongs to.
items.misconception: Thinking any two numbers can be a factor and a multiple as long as they are related somehow.

steps: The factors of 17 are 1 and 17, and 17 is the greater of the two.
The multiples of 17 are 17, 34, 51 and on, and 17 is the first of them.
So the same number closes the list that stops and opens the list that does not.
items.answer: At the top of one and the foot of the other: 17 is the greatest factor of 17 and the smallest multiple of 17
items.question: Where does 17 sit in its own list of factors, and in its own list of multiples?
items.checkpoint: A number is its own greatest factor and its own smallest multiple.
items.misconception: Assuming a number cannot appear in both of its own lists, because the two words sound opposite.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: 7 divides 77 exactly. Say that as a fact about factors and as a fact about multiples.
items.final_answer: 7 is a factor of 77, and 77 is a multiple of 7

items.question: 2 and 23 are a factor pair. Which number do they build, and what is it to them?
items.final_answer: 46, and 46 is a multiple of both 2 and 23

items.question: In the multiplication 8 times 9 is 72, which number is the multiple?
Can 88 be a factor of 44?
items.final_answer: No. 88 is greater than 44, and a factor is never greater than the number it divides. 44 is a factor of 88 instead

items.question: Write all three factor pairs of 20, and say what 20 is to each pair.
items.final_answer: 1 and 20, 2 and 10, and 4 and 5. 20 is the multiple of every one of those pairs

items.question: Name the greatest factor of 34 and the smallest multiple of 34.
A child says 9 is a factor of 6, because 3 divides both of them. What is wrong, and what is true?
items.final_answer: 9 is greater than 6, so it cannot divide 6 exactly. What is true is that 3 is a factor of both 6 and 9

items.question: Which number is both the greatest factor of 65 and its smallest multiple, and what are all four of its factors?
items.final_answer: 65 itself, and its factors are 1, 5, 13 and 65

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: reads one exact division as a factor fact and as a multiple fact
keeps the two readings in one frame once the card has been turned
will not take the word factor or multiple until the number is named
draws the two numbers to scale and refuses a factor bigger than its number
multiplies two numbers out as rows and names the number they build
stands one number at the top of its factor list and the foot of its multiple track
holds the chapter's four words for a partner to be quizzed on

teaching_notes: This is the shortest serves list of the six tools, and that is a fact about the printed chapter rather than about the idea: the section that relates the two words sets no exercise of its own at all. Treat it as the most important twenty minutes anyway, because everything after it depends on the relation being one thing. Make the naming a spoken rule from the first minute. Nobody says factor or multiple in this classroom without saying of what, and the gate should be backed up by insisting on it out loud, because the printed wording will not back it up. Turn one division over and leave both readings up on the stage while the class says them; taking one down turns a single fact back into two things to remember. The size rail is worth doing wrong on purpose. Ask for the bigger number as the factor, let the rail refuse it, and get somebody to say why in their own words. Finish at the own list bay, where a number closes one list and opens the other, and use the word pad for the flashcards with a partner, asking the four words in a different order each time.
generation_prompt: Build a relation tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. One exact division sits on a card in the middle that flips on a tap; one face states it as a fact about factors and the other as a fact about multiples, and once flipped both faces are held side by side inside a single frame rather than one replacing the other. A name it gate guards a writing bay: word tiles reading factor and multiple cannot be dropped into a sentence slot until a number tile naming what they belong to has been placed, and a sentence left incomplete springs back with the empty slot lit. A size rail runs beneath the card drawn strictly to scale, with the two numbers placed along it by size and a factor slot at the smaller end; a bigger number dragged into the factor slot is refused and the rail is redrawn so the difference in length is the explanation. A pair bay takes two numbers, lays them out as equal rows on a ruled board, and returns the number they build labelled as the multiple of both. An own list bay shows one number simultaneously at the closed end of a penned factor list, with a wall drawn past it, and at the first step of a track of multiples that leaves the frame with no end mark. A word pad at the edge holds the chapter's four words for a partner quiz. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Read the division on the card. Turn it over and read it the other way. Keep both readings up together. Never say factor or multiple without saying which number it belongs to. Check the rail: the factor is always the smaller one.
